technique.how: With the patient supine, knees flexed and distracted by conversation, palpate each quadrant gently with a flat hand. Involuntary guarding is reflex contraction of the abdominal wall that persists despite relaxation and distraction; rigidity is a board-like wall that does not soften on expiration.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to lie supine and relax; warm hands; examine tender areas last.
technique.contraindications: None; avoid deep or repeated palpation once peritonitis is evident.

interpretation.positive_finding: Involuntary guarding or rigidity indicates parietal peritoneal irritation (localized or generalized peritonitis) and raises the probability of appendicitis, perforation or other surgical pathology.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of guarding lowers but does not exclude appendicitis (pediatric LR- ~0.6); early, retrocaecal or perforated disease in the elderly or immunosuppressed may show no guarding.
interpretation.pitfalls: Voluntary guarding from anxiety, cold hands or ticklishness mimics the sign; obesity, steroids, opioids and advanced age blunt it. Distinguishing voluntary from involuntary guarding is examiner dependent.
interpretation.changes_what: Present: treat as peritonitis, obtain surgical review and CT urgently. Absent: modest reassurance only; do not use to withhold imaging.

estimates.target_condition: Acute appendicitis (absence of guarding as negative predictor)
estimates.population: 755 children and adolescents (median age 11.9 y) evaluated for suspected appendicitis; 36% had appendicitis
Children and adolescents with proven appendicitis in the same cohort (n=755 enrolled)
estimates.computed_from: sensitivity = 1 - 0.47 (proportion of proven appendicitis cases lacking guarding, reported in abstract)

sources.citation: Kharbanda AB, Taylor GA, Fishman SJ, Bachur RG. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
Andersson RE. Meta-analysis of the clinical and laboratory diagnosis of appendicitis. Br J Surg. 2004;91(1):28-37.
Dixon JM, Elton RA, Rainey JB, Macleod DA. Rectal examination in patients with pain in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. BMJ. 1991;302(6773):386-388.
Wagner JM, McKinney WP, Carpenter JL. Does this patient have appendicitis? JAMA. 1996;276(19):1589-1594.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on absence of guarding to exclude surgical pathology in the elderly, immunosuppressed, obese, pregnant or opioid-treated patient.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Diffuse rigidity with hypotension or fever is generalized peritonitis until proven otherwise: resuscitate, antibiotics, immediate surgical consultation.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Separating voluntary from involuntary guarding is subjective; agreement between examiners is only fair-to-moderate in most series.

extraction_notes: Adult pooled LRs for guarding/rigidity (Wagner 1996 RCE; Andersson 2004 BJS) sit in tables not visible via PubMed/PMC, so they are cited qualitatively only (Andersson abstract: guarding/rigidity among strongest discriminators, ROC 0.68-0.78; Dixon 1991 abstract: OR 3.07 guarding, 5.03 rigidity - odds ratios, not entered as estimates). The only numbers with a visible location are pediatric (Kharbanda 2007): LR- 0.63 for lack of guarding and 47% of proven cases lacking guarding (sensitivity 0.53 computed). Status partially_quantified; a verifier with JAMA/BJS access should add the adult pooled LR+/LR- (expected LR+ ~3-4 for rigidity).
